deck.title: AI-Assisted Embedded Development
deck.subtitle: Driving Devin to build firmware you can defend · ESP32
deck.purpose: Day-0 orientation delivered before any hands-on work. Covers the course thesis, Devin, PlatformIO, the intake framework, the hardware, and the pre-flight checklist.

design_direction.tone: Technical, direct, confident. The audience are senior engineers — no cartoon robots, no hype, no 'AI will replace you' framing.

typography.heading: Inter, IBM Plex Sans, sans-serif
typography.code: JetBrains Mono, IBM Plex Mono, monospace

rules: Max ~6 bullets per slide; short fragments, not sentences.
Every code block uses the monospace family with syntax highlighting.
Warning slides use accent_warning as a left border or badge.
Hardware photos sit on a light neutral card so the dark deck doesn't clash with white product shots.
Never render speaker_notes on the slide.

slides.title: AI-Assisted Embedded Development
slides.subtitle: Driving Devin to build firmware you can defend
slides.meta: 3 days · 9 topics · ESP32 + Grove · Engineer track
slides.speaker_notes: Set the tone in the first 60 seconds: this is not an AI hype course. It is an engineering-discipline course that happens to use an AI agent.

slides.statement:
The AI writes the code.
The engineer owns correctness.
slides.caption: The thesis of this course. We will repeat it daily.
slides.speaker_notes: Say it out loud, then pause. Everything in the next three days derives from this one line.

slides.title: What this course is — and isn't
bullets: **Is:** learning to specify, review and verify AI-generated firmware
**Is:** catching an AI that is confidently wrong about hardware
**Isn't:** C basics, breadboarding, OSI lectures — you already have these
9 topics · ~2 hours each · 3 per day · one new PlatformIO project each
Same objective for everyone; **different code is expected**
slides.speaker_notes: The audience is senior. Say explicitly that we are skipping fundamentals so we can go deep on protocol, concurrency and security.

slides.title: What you should walk away with
rows: you can explain every line the AI wrote
templates you would use at work on Monday
each with the datasheet line that proves it

callout.text: There is no grading on this course. The device is the least valuable of the four — it stays on the bench; the other three come to work with you.

slides.speaker_notes: No assessment means nothing forces the priority except what you visibly value. Land this slide hard, or the room optimises for a demo that lights up.

slides.title: Two artifacts you build all week

columns.heading: Prompt library
columns.body: Every prompt that worked, saved as a reusable template. By T9 you should be reusing templates unedited on new hardware.

columns.heading: Caught-the-AI log
columns.body: Every confident error — **with the datasheet line that proves it** and your fix. Without proof it's an anecdote, not a story.

slides.speaker_notes: Tell them to create both files on Day 1, Topic 1. Retrofitting them on Day 3 is obvious and scores badly.

slides.title: What is Devin?
bullets: An **autonomous AI software engineer** — not autocomplete
You give a goal; it plans, writes files, runs builds, iterates
Running on the free **SWE-1.6** model for this course
Works across your whole project, not just the current buffer
**Your job shifts:** from writing code to specifying, reviewing, verifying
slides.speaker_notes: Many will have used Copilot. Emphasise the difference in scope and initiative — and therefore in where the human effort goes.

slides.title: Where Devin is strong — and where it fails

columns.heading: Genuinely good at
columns.body: Boilerplate and scaffolding · library glue · refactoring · explaining unfamiliar APIs · turning a clear spec into working code fast · iterating on a precise error message

columns.heading: Fails at — and this is the course
columns.body: **Invents hardware facts** — pins, I²C addresses, library names, voltages · writes happy-path only · defaults to blocking `delay()` · has no idea what is physically wired to your board

slides.speaker_notes: The critical nuance: it does not hedge. It states wrong hardware facts plainly and fluently. That is why the datasheet gate exists.

slides.statement:
Treat Devin like a fast, knowledgeable,
overconfident junior engineer
who has never seen your hardware.
slides.caption: Give it a written spec. Review everything against the datasheet.
slides.speaker_notes: This mental model does more work than any other slide. Refer back to it whenever someone is surprised by a hallucinated pin.

slides.title: What is PlatformIO?
bullets: A professional embedded build system inside **VS Code**
**Declared dependencies** — libraries + versions live in `platformio.ini`, in the project
Per-project board, framework, monitor speed, build flags
Real project structure and working IntelliSense
**Reproducible** — a colleague opens your folder and gets your toolchain
slides.speaker_notes: Frame it as 'the Arduino IDE's global library state is why builds differ between machines'. Senior engineers feel that pain immediately.

slides.title: Project layout and platformio.ini
slides.code:
[env:esp32dev]
platform = espressif32
board = esp32dev
framework = arduino
monitor_speed = 115200
lib_deps =
    adafruit/Adafruit NeoPixel
    ; add libraries here as each topic needs them

side_panel.heading: Structure
side_panel.body:
my_project/
├── platformio.ini
├── src/main.cpp
├── include/
├── lib/
└── test/

callout.text: The serial monitor holds the port — close it before uploading.

slides.statement:
Most AI firmware failures
are specification failures.
slides.caption: The AI didn't misunderstand C. It guessed a pin, an address, or a voltage that nobody told it.
slides.speaker_notes: This is the justification for the entire framework. If they accept this sentence, the interview step stops feeling like overhead.

slides.speaker_notes: Walk the loop once. Stress that Step 4 is ONE phase — the most common failure is asking the AI to build everything.

slides.title: Step 0 — you create the project, not the AI
bullets: PlatformIO → New Project → `esp32dev` + Arduino
Set `monitor_speed = 115200`
**Upload something trivial and confirm it runs**
Only then copy in the starter and paste the kickoff prompt

callout.text: A broken build must be unambiguous. You own the environment; the AI owns the code tested against it.

slides.speaker_notes: If the AI also generated platformio.ini, a failure could be code, config, or USB driver. Removing that ambiguity saves hours across nine topics.

slides.title: The datasheet gate — the heart of the framework
bullets: The starter **forbids** the AI assuming any pin, address, voltage, direction or timing
If a document doesn't state it, the AI must **ask** — never guess
Datasheets live in `hardware/` — attach them when asked
Everything downstream inherits errors from `REQUIREMENTS.md` — **read it before approving**
§4 hard constraints and §10 watch-the-AI are the sections that matter

callout.text: Attaching a file is not an instruction. Devin will summarize an attached JSON unless you tell it to act — always paste the kickoff prompt.

slides.title: Repeat runs get faster
bullets: From T2 onward most answers are **"same as \<earlier topic\>"**
Attach that project's `REQUIREMENTS.md` — the AI imports instead of re-interviewing
Target: **10–15 minutes** of interview per topic
Depth goes into whatever is genuinely **new** this topic
Each topic guide has a *suggested answers* table — use the shape, your own words

slides.title: Cytron ROBO ESP32 Rev 1.1

image.alt: Cytron ROBO ESP32 Rev 1.1 carrier board

bullets: Hosts a **30-pin NodeMCU ESP32 DevKit V1**
NeoPixel **D15** · buttons **D34/D35** · buzzer **D23**
Servo headers **D4/D5/D18/D19**
I²C **D21/D22** · UART Grove port **D16/D17**
Grove ports supply **3.3 V**

slides.speaker_notes: There is only ONE I²C Grove port. The OLED owns it for T3–T7; the gesture sensor takes it from T8 and the device goes headless — the T6 dashboard becomes the display. One physical swap, never both at once, so no hub or QWIIC cable is needed.

slides.title: The seven constraints that break builds
slides.subtitle: Every one is a documented datasheet fact. Every one is something the AI gets wrong.

items.text: **ADC2 dies when WiFi is on.** Analog on **ADC1 (D32/D33)**. Works Day 1, garbage Day 2 — looks exactly like a software bug.
**D34/D35 are input-only, no pull-up.** `pinMode(34, INPUT_PULLUP)` is invalid — the AI writes it almost every time.
**DHT11 is digital 1-wire, not I²C.** Address `0x38` is the DHT20 — a different part.
**RS485 is half-duplex.** Two nodes, one pair, one talker at a time.
**The board is 3.3 V.** ESP32 inputs are not 5 V tolerant — this is why 5 V-only Grove modules are not in the kit, and why the servo is a 3–6 V TS90A rather than a 4.8 V SG90.
**No `delay()` in the main loop.** Non-blocking only — `millis()`, later FreeRTOS.

slides.speaker_notes: Do not rush this slide. Every trap in the nine topics traces back to one of these seven lines.

slides.title: Before Day 1 — setup checklist
items: **One project built and uploaded successfully** — downloads the ESP32 toolchain (slow, once) and proves your USB drivers work
Kit checked against the six modules listed in the README
Skimmed `hardware/kit_reference_sheet.md` — every pin, address and gotcha on one page

callout.text: Do not skip the trial upload. Discovering a driver problem at 09:05 on Day 1 costs the whole room.

slides.title: Mindset for the week
bullets: **Compiling is not working.** Working is verified on hardware, against the datasheet.
**Read `REQUIREMENTS.md` before approving it** — everything inherits its errors.
**When the AI is confidently wrong, that's a deliverable** — capture it with proof.
**Ask "what breaks in production?"** about every piece of code it hands you.
**Descoping is engineering** — a deliberate cut is a good decision, not a failure.
slides.closing_statement: Nine times this week the AI will state a hardware fact with total confidence and be wrong. Every one is catchable by reading the datasheet. That habit — not any single device — is what you take back to work on Monday.
slides.speaker_notes: End on the closing statement, then go straight into T1. Do not take a long Q&A here; the questions answer themselves in Topic 1.
